“Word families” are not the same across languages. And that matters for how we talk about the Science of Reading. In English, word families are typically about sound patterns: cat, bat, hat They help students recognize rimes and decode efficiently. In Spanish, familias de palabras are about meaning and structure: pan, panadero, panadería They help students understand how words are built and how meaning travels across forms. Same term. Different linguistic logic. Here is where this connects to the Science of Reading. The Science of Reading is grounded in how reading develops within a language system. But when we move across languages, we are not just applying the same practices in translation. We are working across different orthographies, different linguistic structures, and different pathways to meaning. English opaque orthography needs pattern recognition to support decoding. Spanish is a more transparent orthography, where morphology and meaning are more consistently visible. So when we treat “word families” as equivalent across languages, we risk doing two things: • Importing English phonics practices into Spanish without alignment • Missing the opportunity to leverage the strengths of Spanish for vocabulary and meaning making For multilingual learners, this is not a small shift. It is the difference between teaching toward the structure of the language and teaching against it. A cross-linguistic Science of Reading asks us to be more precise: Not just “what works” But “what works, in which language, and why” Because biliteracy is not built through replication. It is built through alignment. #ScienceOfReading #Biliteracy #MultilingualLearners #LiteracyLeadership #EquityInEducation ...more ...more

Interpreter vs. Translator — what’s the difference? This question comes up often, and it’s a very common one. Both interpreters and translators support communication across languages, but they do so in slightly different ways: Interpreters work with spoken language • Meetings • Evaluations • Trainings • Conferences • Phone or virtual conversations Translators work with written documents • Birth and marriage certificates • Educational and legal documents • Forms, letters, and reports Both roles require specialized training, accuracy, and attention to confidentiality — and knowing which service is needed helps ensure communication is clear and complete. If you’re ever unsure whether interpretation or translation is the right fit for a particular situation, I’m always happy to help clarify or talk it through. — Tammy Pérez Spanish–English Interpreter & Translator Pérez Language Solutions Servicios de interpretación y traducción al español disponibles. #LanguageAccess #SpanishInterpreter #TranslationServices ...more

I remember the day we bought our "$8k Lamborghini" In the early 90's our team and I had just launched the Leadership College and our budget was meager to say the least. Like trying to squeeze a dollar out of 15 cents! We had this vision to send teams into schools to talk to students about purpose and value, and no vehicle to actually get there. When our Finance Director called, they told us about an old 15 passenger Dodge van for sale at a mom-and-pop lot in Rockford. He figured the church could swing it cost wise, and when we pulled up that thing was U-G-L-Y. But it ran, and it drove well. $8K later, we pulled off the lot with it and we felt like purchased a Lamborghini. The vision now had a vehicle. Somebody helped us rig up a janky sound system and we were off to make a difference in as many student's lives as possible. One school booked us. Then another. And another. Our program interacted with over 1 million students during the next decade in large part to that ugly brown van, better known as our "$8K Lamborghini" Eventually our budget grew, better equipment followed, and our modes of transportation received a necessary upgrades. But here's what I learned: Big vision often begins with small steps God also honors those small and consistent steps of obedience and consistency...in church we'd call that "faithfulness to your calling". Maybe you find yourself walking this out today and I'd encourage you not to underestimate the seemingly small things like an act of obedience, a heartfelt prayer, or a necessary decision made. If you don't embrace the process, you'll never sustain the outcome. Be careful not to call something "insignificant" if God calls it a "beginning"

I thought I already knew what good academic writing was, having achieved a high score in the writing component of the IELTS. To my understanding, that was proof of my advanced writing skill before starting my Master of Applied Linguistics at the University of Melbourne. I assumed strong writing meant correct grammar, varied syntax, and rich vocabulary. One semester into the programme, I discovered that those are the least of your problems. One of the subjects that challenged me most in my first semester was Presenting Academic Discourse, a course that covers a wide range of academic writing genres and skills, including critical reviews, literature reviews, academic style and register, structuring arguments, managing reader expectations, and delivering seminar presentations. We were not only introduced to these genres throughout the course, we were actually required to produce them in multiple assignments. What really made the difference is that I came to understand what academic writing actually demands. It was not just the ability to express ideas, but the ability to construct them in a way that guides the reader, meets their expectations, and leaves no room for confusion. One important lesson I learned from this subject that no previous writing class ever taught me: Your reader has expectations, and you are responsible for meeting them. Every sentence sets up what the next one should do. Every paragraph signals what the section is about. Effective academic writers do not just have ideas. They guide their reader through those ideas. This completely shifted how I think about writing. Applying all of this was not easy at first. Being cohesive and coherent at every level of writing simultaneously is a skill that takes deliberate practice. I completed this subject with an H2A grade. It may not be a High Distinction, but the improvement in my scores from the first assignment to the final one tells a story that a single grade cannot. That progression is exactly why I am doing this degree. WAM is undeniably a key indicator of academic performance, but growth is what I am here for. ...more

activity.title: This wonderful new short film perfectly illustrates the predicament we put children in, in the name of "connecting the world." It's by Smartphone Free Childhood , the UK organization founded a month before "The Anxious Generation" came out — it's been wonderful to see them bring parents together to restore healthy childhood. With the UK government expected to announce new restrictions on social media access for under-16s in the coming days, SFC has been instrumental in building the momentum that helped bring us to this moment. They also have a US org, Smartphone Free Childhood US , as well as 45 others across the world. This short film was a pro-bono project by filmmakers, creatives, and SFC supporters who brought this concept to life — and helped get it into cinemas across the UK from next week! Special shoutouts to Arts & Sciences , David Dearlove , James Bland , Charlie Orr , Kwok Yau, Linda Wu, Max Windows, Stitch Editing, Black Kite Studios , 750mph , Twenty Below Music 👏🏼 And of course, thank you SFC founders and directors Daisy Greenwell and Joe Ryrie 👏🏼 You can watch the full film in horizontal format, as it was originally made, on Smartphone-Free Childhood's site — linked in comments. And you can watch it in theaters in the UK! If you repost the film, please credit Smartphone Free Childhood . And If you'd like to get involved in the movement, you can find a Smartphone-Free Childhood national chapter wherever you are!

One of the most common arguments for classroom technology is this: “If students need digital literacy, shouldn’t technology be integrated across every subject?” I don’t think those are the same question. In this clip from a recent AMA session, I discuss the difference between curriculum and pedagogy — and why teaching digital skills does not automatically justify teaching everything through computers. There’s a major difference between: • teaching students how technology works and • making technology the foundation of every learning experience. The distinction matters more than ever. #Education #EdTech #DigitalLiteracy #Teaching #Learning #Neuroscience #Schools

I can’t let #BannedBooksWeek end without revisiting a truth that still stings: Culturally Responsive Teaching & The Brain, the book I wrote in 2014 to elevate culture as a cognitive asset and build the skill and capacity of educators to teach with both care and push so students build the muscle to reclaim their learning power, remains banned in seven state departments of education. But, it’s not just my book. The diverse narratives of gifted writers, ideas about inclusion, and the straight truth about U.S. history are being kept from children. Our students need the words and stories that wake them up to their power, or the cycle of harm keeps repeating. Remember, freedom ain’t free. What can you do? There’s plenty. If you have 5, 15, or 30 minutes, learn about the actions you can take to stand up against censorship in #education by joining in on today’s #LetFreedomReadDay ( https://lnkd.in/gxyKUZUJ ) efforts. And, if you’re looking for the next step in disrupting cognitive redlining, pick up my newest, Rebuilding Students’ Learning Power: Teaching for Instructional Equity and Cognitive Justice to go deeper into the how and tap into its good trouble: bit.ly/3UT9rmZ #Pedagogy #Books #Learning

One important lesson I learned from this subject that no previous writing class ever taught me: Your reader has expectations, and you are responsible for meeting them. Every sentence sets up what the next one should do. Every paragraph signals what the section is about. Effective academic writers do not just have ideas. They guide their reader through those ideas. This completely shifted how I think about writing. Applying all of this was not easy at first. Being cohesive and coherent at every level of writing simultaneously is a skill that takes deliberate practice. I completed this subject with an H2A grade. It may not be a High Distinction, but the improvement in my scores from the first assignment to the final one tells a story that a single grade cannot. That progression is exactly why I am doing this degree. WAM is undeniably a key indicator of academic performance, but growth is what I am here for. ...more

raw.about: I am an English Language Consultant with a background in applied linguistics, English grammar, and second language acquisition. I hold a Bachelor of Arts in English Literature and Linguistics and have over eight years of experience working across ESL/EFL contexts, including exam preparation, adult education, and online language learning platforms. While my professional background includes extensive classroom instruction, my current focus is on language analysis, content quality, and learning design rather than direct teaching. My work involves reviewing and improving English learning materials, advising on grammar accuracy and clarity, and applying classroom- and e-learning-informed insight to enhance online language learning experiences. Through years of hands-on experience with digital platforms, I have developed a strong understanding of what is effective in e-learning environments and how learners engage with language content. I am particularly interested in the structure of English, common learner difficulties, and how linguistic principles can be applied to create clearer, more effective learning experiences. My consulting work is grounded in real classroom and e-learning experience and focuses on improving quality, consistency, and learner outcomes.

activity.title: What is a Teaching Portfolio? 7 Great Resources to Use for Creating a Teaching Portfolio A teaching portfolio (or dossier) is a coherent set of material representing your teaching practice related to student learning. “Teaching practice” broadly extends beyond the obvious activities that go into teaching a course to include all activities that enrich student learning. Teaching portfolios vary considerably depending on their specific purpose, audience, institutional context, and individual needs. However, the body of a portfolio is generally about 5-8 pages long and is followed by appendices, which usually make up about 8-15 more pages. Your portfolio would likely include a summary of your teaching experience and responsibilities, a reflective statement of your teaching philosophy and goals, a brief discussion of your teaching methods and strategies, as well as activities undertaken to improve teaching, and a statement of goals and plans for the future. The appendices would consist of supplemental materials that further document or support the information you provide in the body of your portfolio. A course portfolio, which focuses on a single course, has many features and benefits in common with a teaching portfolio. Although we do not discuss course portfolios in this handbook, much of the information here can be applied to developing one. 1.
